extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates and graduate students studying set theory / model theory / forcing
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter covering cardinal arithmetic, cofinality, models of ZFC, the Levy hierarchy, elementarity/Tarski–Vaught, Mostowski collapse, constructions of countable transitive models, and the basics of forcing (posets, dense sets, generic filters). Intended as a textbook treatment to teach definitions, theorems, and proof ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation guideline: separate symbols for ordinals and cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ω for the ordinal {0,1,...} and ℵ0 for the same set viewed as a cardinal; be explicit whether ordinal or cardinal arithmetic is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes this is an intentional abuse of notation commonly encountered, and to combat confusion the text uses ω for ordinals and ℵα for cardinals; e.g., ω·ω = ω^2 (ordinal) but ℵ0·ℵ0 = ℵ0 (cardinal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: ordinal associated to a cardinal (ω^α)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let ω^α = ℵ^α viewed as an ordinal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention is adopted to refer unambiguously to the ordinal that corresponds to a given cardinal ℵα when needed in ordinal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite cardinals squared (Theorem 91.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If κ is an infinite cardinal then κ·κ = κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: order κ×κ by <_max where (α1,β1) <_max (α2,β2) iff max{α1,β1} < max{α2,β2} or equal and lexicographic; this is a well-order in bijection with some ordinal γ, and transfinite induction shows |γ| ≤ κ so |κ×κ| ≤ κ. For ℵ0 the usual diagonal argument is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite cardinal addition/multiplication (Theorem 91.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given cardinals κ and µ, one of which is infinite, κ·µ = κ + µ = max{κ,µ}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: max{κ,µ} ≤ κ+µ ≤ κ·µ ≤ max{κ,µ}·max{κ,µ} = max{κ,µ}; hence equality holds. This shows cardinal addition/multiplication are 'boring' when at least one factor is infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: cardinal exponentiation (Definition 91.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For cardinals κ and λ, κ^λ := |F(λ, κ)| where F(λ, κ) is the set of functions from λ to κ. In particular 2^κ = |P(κ)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abuse-of-notation warning: same notation used for ordinal exponentiation in other contexts; cardinal exponentiation behaves differently (e.g., 2^ℵ0 > ℵ0), and the Continuum Hypothesis 2^ℵ0 = ℵ1 is independent of ZFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: cofinal map (Definition 91.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let λ be an ordinal and α another ordinal. A map f: α → λ is cofinal if for every λ' < λ there exists some α' ∈ α with f(α') ≥ λ'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informally, f 'reaches arbitrarily high' into λ. Examples: n ↦ ω^n is cofinal ω→ω^ω; identity map α→α is cofinal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: cofinality (Definition 91.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a limit ordinal λ, cof(λ) is the smallest ordinal α such that there exists a cofinal map α → λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: cof(λ) must be an infinite cardinal. When taking cofinality of a cardinal κ, one often asks whether cof(κ) = κ (regular) or < κ (singular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular vs singular cardinal (examples and criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A cardinal κ is regular iff cof(κ) = κ; otherwise it is singular (cofinality < κ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cof(ℵ0)=ℵ0 so ℵ0 is regular; cof(ℵ1)=ℵ1 so ℵ1 regular (argument: countable union of countables is countable); ℵω is singular with cof(ℵω)=ℵ0 since ℵ0<ℵ1<... approaches ℵω. Theorem: successor cardinals are regular (proof mirrors ℵ1 case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: strong limit cardinal
rubrics_metrics.description: An infinite cardinal κ is a strong limit cardinal if for all κ' < κ, 2^{κ'} < κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ℵ0 is a strong limit cardinal. Remark: any strong limit cardinal must be a limit cardinal (exercise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: (weakly/strongly) inaccessible cardinals
rubrics_metrics.description: A regular limit cardinal other than ℵ0 is called weakly inaccessible. A regular strong limit cardinal other than ℵ0 is called strongly inaccessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cardinals are 'large' and their existence cannot be proved in ZFC. Example: if κ is strongly inaccessible then V_κ is a model of ZFC (Problem 92D⋆).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levy hierarchy classification rule (§92.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulas with only bounded quantifiers are Δ0 = Σ0 = Π0. If ψ is Π_n then ∃x1...∃xk ψ is Σ_{n+1}; if ψ is Σ_n then ∀x1...∀xk ψ is Π_{n+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounded quantifiers (e.g. ∃a ∈ x, ∀a ∈ x) produce absoluteness over transitive models. Examples: isEmpty(x) and x⊆y are Δ0; 'y = P(x)' is Π1; PowerSet axiom is Π3. Only alternating unbounded quantifier count matters because multiple existentials can be combined via pairing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: model (Definition 92.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A model M consists of a set M and a binary relation E ⊆ M×M which interprets '∈' inside the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tuple (M,E) is used; often one considers transitive models (M,∈) where E is actual membership restricted to M. Examples: (ω,∈) is a 'stupid' but instructive model for checking which ZFC axioms hold inside M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: satisfaction relation M ⊨ φ[b1,...,bn] (Definition 92.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction is defined by induction on formula complexity: atomic cases x=y and x∈y interpreted via equality and E; Boolean connectives via truth values; ∃xψ holds iff there exists b∈M with M ⊨ ψ[b,...].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key point: quantifiers range over M, so the set M is used only when evaluating ∃ and ∀. Parameters must be elements of M. This definition underlies all notions of 'model of ZFC'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: model of ZFC and inner model (Definitions 92.2.5, 92.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A model of ZFC is a model M=(M,E) satisfying all ZFC axioms. An inner model is a transitive model of ZFC (abbreviated as M when transitive and E is ∈).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitive models are especially convenient because many formulas become absolute; Mostowski collapse can convert many well-founded extensional models to transitive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absoluteness facts and examples (§92.3 and exercises)
rubrics_metrics.description: Δ0 formulas (bounded quantifiers) are absolute between transitive models; Σ1 formulas are upward-preserved: if M1 ⊨ Σ1[b] then M2 ⊨ Σ1[b] for M1⊆M2; Π1 formulas are downward-preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exercises: 'x is an ordinal' and 'x is transitive' are Δ0; 'x is countable' is Σ1; 'y = P(x)' is Π1. These facts explain phenomena like (ω,∈) satisfying PowerSet relative to its own small universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: substructure and elementary substructure (Definitions 92.4.1–92.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: M1 ⊆ M2 means M1⊆M2 and relations agree. M1 ≺ M2 (elementary substructure) iff for every formula φ(x1,...,xn) and parameters from M1, M1 ⊨ φ iff M2 ⊨ φ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: elementarity fails only due to unbounded quantifiers/witnesses; bounded quantifiers won't cause disagreement. Concrete analogy: MIT⊆Massachusetts but MIT isn't elementary in MA because existential witnesses in the larger structure may have no counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarski–Vaught test (Lemma 92.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For M1⊆M2, M1 ≺ M2 iff for every formula φ(x,params) and params in M1, whenever M2 has a witness  b̃ ∈ M2 with M2 ⊨ φ(b̃,params), there exists b ∈ M1 with M1 ⊨ φ(b,params).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tool to verify elementarity by showing witnesses can be 'pulled down' into the substructure. Proof by induction on formula complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure criteria for transitive sets to satisfy ZFC axioms (Lemma 92.5.1 items i–vi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be a nonempty transitive set. Then: (i) M satisfies Extensionality, Foundation, EmptySet. (ii) M ⊨ Pairing if x,y∈M ⇒ {x,y}∈M. (iii) M ⊨ Union if x∈M ⇒ ⋃x ∈ M. (iv) M ⊨ PowerSet if x∈M ⇒ P(x)∩M ∈ M. (v) M ⊨ Replacement if for every x∈M and every M-definable function F:x→M (with parameters) we have F''(x) ∈ M. (vi) M ⊨ Infinity if ω ∈ M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces verifying axioms to checking natural closure properties of M under the relevant set-formation operations and definable images. Note converses hold except for (vi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mostowski collapse lemma (Lemma 92.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X=(X,∈) is a set-model satisfying Extensionality, then there exists a unique isomorphism π:X→M for a transitive model M=(M,∈) (the transitive collapse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via transfinite recursion π(x):={π(y)|y∈x}. Uniqueness and existence rely on well-foundedness and extensionality. Practical use: convert well-founded extensional models to transitive ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of a countable transitive model assuming an inaccessible (Theorem 92.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming ZFC+ (existence of a strongly inaccessible κ) there exists a transitive countable model X of ZFC. Construct X as an increasing union X = ⋃_n X_n adding witnesses for formulas with parameters at each stage, then apply Mostowski collapse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key steps: start with X_0 = ∅, at stage n add elements b∈V_κ witnessing any formula ϕ[b,params] with params in X_n; each X_n remains countable; union satisfies Tarski–Vaught and then collapse to transitive. Proof uses Choice (Skolem functions) to select witnesses. This is the usual downward Löwenheim–Skolem/Skolem hull method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downward Löwenheim–Skolem / Skolem hull theorem (Theorem 92.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a model M=(M,E) and A⊆M there is B (Skolem hull of A) with A⊆B⊆M, (B,E)≺M, and |B| = max{ω,|A|}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The textbook construction used in Theorem 92.7.1 is the special case A=∅. Skolem functions f_φ can be pre-chosen to witness existential formulas; Choice is used for simultaneous selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skolem paradox / non-absoluteness of 'countable' (§92.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: A transitive model M can be a countable set in the external universe V yet satisfy 'there exists an uncountable set'; countability is a Σ1 notion and thus not absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: M can have x which in V is countable via some injective f:x→ω, but f may not belong to M. Thus M ⊨ 'x is uncountable' because M's ∀f only ranges over M's functions. This explains how M can think it has smallest uncountable cardinal ℵ1^M while externally that ordinal is countable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: formula absoluteness examples (§92.3 and Problem 92B)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ is Δ0 then M1 ⊨ ϕ[params] ⇔ M2 ⊨ ϕ[params] for M1⊆M2; if ϕ is Σ1 then M1 ⊨ ϕ ⇒ M2 ⊨ ϕ; if ϕ is Π1 then M2 ⊨ ϕ ⇒ M1 ⊨ ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These monotonicity/absoluteness patterns are consequences of the Levy hierarchy definitions and are used repeatedly in model-theoretic arguments about transitive models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: dense subset of a poset (Definition 93.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a partial order P, a subset D⊆P is dense if for all p∈P there exists q∈D with q ≤ p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dense sets are the requirements a generic filter must meet; examples: whole P is dense, any downward slice is dense. In 2^{<ω} sets like 'strings ending with 001' are dense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: compatibility and incompatibility in posets (Definition 93.1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For p,q ∈ P, p ∥ q iff there exists r ≤ p,q (they are compatible); otherwise p ⊥ q (incompatible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compatibility expresses 'can be extended simultaneously'. In the infinite binary tree 2^{<ω} no two distinct nodes are compatible unless one extends the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: filter and M-generic filter (Definition 93.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonempty set G⊆P is a filter if (a) upwards-closed: ∀p∈G ∀q≥p (q∈G) and (b) every pair of elements of G are compatible. G is M-generic if for every dense D∈M, G∩D ≠ ∅.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1_P (maximum element) is always in a filter. Generic filters 'hit' every dense set coded in the ground model M; in 2^{<ω} a generic filter corresponds to a binary sequence containing every finite string as substring (informal 'looks random'). If G∈M then G cannot be M-generic (since P ackslash G is a dense set in M hitting which would contradict).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rasiowa–Sikorski lemma (Lemma 93.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a countable transitive model of ZFC and P∈M is a partial order, then there exists an M-generic filter G⊆P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: diagonalize/hit dense sets one by one (countably many). This is why forcing arguments often assume M countable to produce generics externally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: splitting poset (Definition 93.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial order P is splitting if for every p∈P there exist q,r ≤ p with q ⊥ r (i.e., p can be extended incompatibly in at least two ways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Splitting ensures nontrivial branching; used to guarantee that adding a generic will introduce genuinely new objects (e.g., reals) and often to avoid trivial generics like the unique generic on an infinite chain.
